title: Liquids up close: why water pushes harder the deeper you go

summary.text: Poke three holes in a bottle, one high, one in the middle and one low, and fill it with water. The lowest hole squirts the farthest. A thin tube of water and a huge wide tank can push on their bottoms with exactly the same strength, if the water is equally deep. A tap on the top floor of a building runs slowly when the roof tank is nearly empty, though the tank is big. Your child tests where water pushes hardest, marks a level line along a wall with a hose, and finds out why a push on a liquid in a closed pipe goes everywhere. It explains rooftop tanks, dams, car brakes and the deep sea.
summary.art: A plastic bottle on a stool in a bathroom with three jets of water arching from three holes at different heights, the lowest jet landing farthest.

intro.hook: Poke three holes in a plastic bottle, one near the top, one in the middle and one near the bottom. Fill the bottle with water. All three jets start at once. Which one will squirt the farthest?
intro.text: Many people guess the top hole, because it is higher. The answer comes from something you cannot see: the push that water makes on everything it touches. In this unit you measure that push with a bottle, and with a hose that is longer than a room. You find out why the push grows with depth, why it does not depend on how much water there is, and why the water in a hose always settles to the same level. You also build a machine from two syringes, and see why the top-floor tap runs slowly and why a dam is thickest at the bottom.
intro.art: A child crouching beside a stool in a bathroom, watching three arcs of water from a plastic bottle land on a strip of wet newspaper.

outcomes: I can describe liquid particles: they touch and slide, so a liquid takes the shape of its container and keeps its size.
I can say what pressure is, and explain that water pushes on everything it touches, in every direction.
I can show with a bottle that the push of water grows with depth, and explain it as the weight of the water above.
I can explain that the push at a depth depends on the depth only, not on the amount of water beside it or the shape of its container.
I can show that water finds its own level in joined containers, and use this to explain roof tanks, taps and a mason's water level.
I can explain how a push on a liquid in a closed pipe goes everywhere, and how a hydraulic machine uses this to lift a heavy load.
I can explain why dams are thickest at the bottom, and why divers and deep-sea animals feel a bigger push the deeper they go.
I can tell how people worked out that the push depends on depth and not on the amount or shape of the water.

terms.meaning: A liquid keeps its size but takes the shape of its container. Its particles touch each other and slide past each other.
terms.example: Water takes the shape of a tumbler and keeps the same amount.
terms.art: Water in a tumbler and in a bowl, with a zoomed-in circle showing close, jumbled particles.

terms.meaning: A force is a push or a pull. A force can start something moving, stop it or change its shape.
terms.example: You use a force when you push a door open.
terms.art: A child pushing a door open, with an arrow showing the push.

terms.meaning: Pressure is how hard something pushes on each small part of a surface. A big force on a tiny area makes a big pressure.
terms.example: A pin goes into a notice board easily, because all the push of your thumb is on its tiny point.
terms.art: A pin and a thumbtack pushed into a board, with arrows showing the push on the point.

terms.meaning: Depth is how far down something is below the top of the water.
terms.example: A coin at the bottom of a bucket 30 centimetres deep is at a depth of 30 centimetres.
terms.art: A bucket of water with a coin at the bottom and a ruler marking the depth from the surface.

terms.meaning: Weight is the pull of gravity on something. The more stuff, the more weight.
terms.example: A full bucket of water weighs more than an empty one.
terms.art: A hand lifting a full bucket, with an arrow pointing down.

terms.meaning: A jet is a narrow stream of liquid that shoots out of a small hole under pressure.
terms.example: Water squirts as a jet from a hole in a bottle.
terms.art: A bottle with a hole and a thin stream of water arching out.

terms.meaning: The level of a liquid is the height of its top surface. Water that can flow freely settles to the same level everywhere it is joined.
terms.example: The water in the spout of a kettle stands as high as the water inside the kettle.
terms.art: A kettle with a line across its spout and its body at the same height.

terms.meaning: An overhead tank is a big water tank high on a roof. It sends water down to the taps below by the push of its own water.
terms.example: Many homes in India have a plastic tank on the terrace.
terms.art: A black plastic water tank on a terrace with a pipe going down the side of the building.

terms.meaning: Hydraulic means worked by a liquid in a closed pipe. A push at one end moves something at the other end.
terms.example: A car's brakes are hydraulic. Your foot pushes a liquid, and the liquid pushes the brakes.
terms.art: A foot pressing a brake pedal with a tube of liquid to a wheel.

terms.meaning: A piston is a plunger that fits tightly in a tube and moves in and out. The plunger of a syringe is a piston.
terms.example: The plunger of a syringe or a bicycle pump is a piston.
terms.art: A syringe with its plunger labelled piston.

terms.meaning: A dam is a wall built across a river to hold water back.
terms.example: Mettur Dam holds back the Kaveri river in Tamil Nadu.
terms.art: A concrete dam across a river with water behind it.

terms.meaning: Incompressible means that it cannot be squeezed into a smaller space. A liquid is very nearly incompressible, because its particles already touch.
terms.example: You cannot squeeze the water in a full closed bottle into a smaller space.
terms.art: A full sealed bottle with a hand squeezing it, and a label that says cannot squeeze.

terms.meaning: Air pressure is the push of the air on everything. We live at the bottom of a deep sea of air, so it pushes on us all the time.
terms.example: Air pressure pushes the juice up a straw when you drink.
terms.art: A glass of juice with a straw and arrows from the air pushing down on the juice.

terms.meaning: A siphon is a tube that carries a liquid up over a rim and down to a lower place, once it is full.
terms.example: A siphon can empty a water drum into a bucket on the floor.
terms.art: A water drum on a table with a tube running over the rim into a bucket on the floor.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same, so that you know what made the difference.
terms.example: To test the three holes, the bottle, the water and the stool stay the same, and only the height of the hole changes.
terms.art: Three bottles with holes at different heights, standing on the same stool.

terms.meaning: Blood pressure is the push of your blood on the walls of the tubes it flows through. Your heart makes it.
terms.example: A doctor measures blood pressure with a cuff round your arm.
terms.art: A doctor wrapping a cuff round a child's arm.

terms.meaning: A mason is a builder who lays bricks and stones. Masons need walls and floors that are level.
terms.example: A mason uses a water level to check that two ends of a wall are at the same height.
terms.art: A mason with a trowel at a wall, holding a clear hose with water in it.

explanations.concept: Liquids: particles that touch and slide
explanations.definition: In a liquid the particles touch their neighbours and slide past them. So a liquid flows, takes the shape of its container, keeps its size and cannot be squeezed into a smaller space.
explanations.description: The particles of a liquid are packed about as close as in a solid, but they are not locked in place. They slide and tumble over each other. This is why a liquid pours and fills the bottom of a container first. Because the particles are already touching, you cannot push them much closer, so a liquid keeps its size when it moves from one container to another. Pour a litre of water from a jug into a wide dish, and it is still a litre.
examples: A cup of water poured into a plate is still a cup of water.
A sealed bottle full of water is very hard to squash.
Milk, juice, oil and honey all flow, but at different speeds.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in circle of liquid, with touching particles in a jumble and short arrows showing them sliding.
explanations.context: This card says what a liquid is like at the level of particles, because the rest of the unit builds on it.

explanations.concept: Pressure: the push on each small bit of a surface
explanations.definition: Pressure is how hard something pushes on each small part of a surface. It depends on the force and on the area it is spread over.
explanations.description: Stand on one foot and then on two. Your weight is the same, but on one foot it is pressed on a smaller area, so the pressure on the floor is bigger. A pin has a tiny point, so your thumb pushes it into a board easily. A flat thumb on the board does nothing. Scientists measure pressure as force divided by area. A camel has wide feet, so the pressure on the sand is small and the camel does not sink. A nail on a bed of nails has the same force spread over hundreds of points.
examples: A sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one, because the edge is thin.
A camel's wide feet spread her weight and stop her sinking into the sand.
A tractor with wide tyres sinks less in a wet paddy field than a tractor with narrow tyres.
explanations.art: A girl standing on one foot and on two feet on soft sand, with deeper footprints for one foot.
explanations.context: This card explains what pressure means.

explanations.concept: Water pushes on everything it touches, in every direction
explanations.definition: Water pushes on every surface it touches. The push is sideways on a wall, upwards under a boat and downwards on the bottom. It is always at a right angle to the surface.
explanations.description: A liquid cannot hold its own shape, so its particles press against whatever holds them in. Every wall of a container feels this push. In a bottle with holes in the side, the jets leave straight out from the wall, and not downwards. If you hold your hand flat in water, you feel the water on every side. The push at one point is the same in every direction. This is why a tank wall bulges out under the water. It is also why a fish feels the push all over her body, and not only from above.
examples: The side of a full bucket bulges a little under the water.
Jets leave a bottle at a right angle to the wall, whichever way the holes face.
A boat is pushed up by the water under it.
explanations.art: A bottle with four holes in a ring, and water jets leaving straight out in four directions.
explanations.context: This card explains that a liquid pushes in every direction, not only downwards.

explanations.definition: The deeper you go in water, the bigger the push. The push at any depth is the weight of the water above, pressing on each small part.
explanations.description: Imagine a column of water standing on one square centimetre of the bottom. The deeper it is, the taller the column, and the more it weighs. So the push on that square centimetre is bigger. Every 10 metres of water adds about the push of the whole air above us. That push is about the weight of a one-kilogram bag on each square centimetre. So at 10 metres under water, the total push is about double what it is at the surface. At 20 metres it is about three times. This is why your ears hurt in the deep end of a swimming pool.
examples: The lowest hole in a bottle squirts the strongest jet.
A swimmer feels a bigger push on the ears at 3 metres than at 1 metre.
A water pipe at the bottom of a tall tank must be stronger than one at the top.
explanations.art: A tall tank with arrows of push on its side, short arrows near the top and long arrows near the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains why pressure goes up with depth.

explanations.concept: Depth matters, not the amount or the shape
explanations.definition: The push at a depth in water depends only on how deep it is. It does not depend on how much water there is, or on the shape of the container.
explanations.description: A tall thin tube of water 1 metre deep and a wide lake 1 metre deep make the same push at 1 metre down. This surprises many people. The reason is that only the water straight above a point presses on it. The water to the side is held up by the tube wall, or by the water next to it, which pushes on it from the side with the same push. The lake presses on a much bigger area, so its total force on its bottom is larger. But the pressure, the push on each small bit, is the same. This is sometimes called the hydrostatic paradox.
examples: A puddle 5 centimetres deep and a swimming pool 5 centimetres deep push equally on the bottom, bit for bit.
A thin tube 10 metres tall can burst a strong barrel at the bottom, as the story of Pascal tells.
A tall narrow glass of juice pushes harder on its base than a shallow wide plate of juice.
explanations.art: A thin tall tube and a wide tank of the same water depth, both showing the same arrow on the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains the surprising rule that depth, and not the amount, sets the push.

explanations.definition: Water that is free to flow in joined containers settles at the same height in all of them, whatever their shapes and widths.
explanations.description: Join a thin tube and a wide bucket with a hose, and the water stands at the same height in both. If one side were higher, the water at the bottom would be pushed harder on that side, and it would flow towards the lower side until the push was equal. Equal push at the same depth means the same height. Masons use a clear hose full of water to mark two spots on a wall at exactly the same height, even if they are many metres apart. A kettle's spout and body also show it, because the water in the spout stands as high as the water inside.
examples: The water in the spout of a kettle stands as high as the water in the body.
A mason's water level hose marks two points at the same height on a long wall.
The water in a house's pipes rises to the level of the water in the roof tank.
explanations.art: A U-shaped clear hose with a wide funnel on one end and a thin end on the other and the water at the same height in both.
explanations.context: This card explains why water settles at the same level.

explanations.concept: Why the top-floor tap runs slowly
explanations.definition: The push that sends water out of a tap comes from the height of the water in the tank above it. A tap close below the tank gets only a small push, and a tap far below gets a big one.
explanations.description: A roof tank sends water down by the push of its own water. A tap one floor below the tank has only a little depth of water pushing on it. A tap on the ground floor, many metres lower, has a much bigger push. So when the water in the tank falls low, the top-floor tap suffers most. The ground-floor tap hardly notices. That is why top floors have weak taps in the morning, when the tank has been emptied. Pumps, taller tank stands and keeping the tank full can all help. Narrow pipes and many taps open at once also reduce the flow.
examples: A bucket of water held high drains faster through a tube than one held low.
Houses at the bottom of a hill get stronger water pressure than houses at the top.
A water tower is built high, so that taps far away still get a good push.
explanations.art: A tall building with a roof tank, and thick arrows of water push at the ground-floor tap and thin ones at the top-floor tap.
explanations.context: This card explains why taps in tall buildings run at different strengths.

explanations.concept: Dams and pipes: stronger at the bottom
explanations.definition: The push of water is biggest at the bottom, so dams are thickest at the bottom, and pipes and tanks must be strongest there.
explanations.description: A wall holding back deep water feels a push that grows with depth. At the top it is small. Near the bottom it is huge. So a dam is built wide at the base and narrower at the top. The Kallanai, or Grand Anicut, is a stone weir across the Kaveri river in Tamil Nadu. It was built about two thousand years ago, and it is traditionally credited to the Chola king Karikalan. It is still in use today. Tall modern dams, such as the Tehri Dam in the Himalayas, which is about 260 metres tall, follow the rule that a dam is widest at the bottom.
examples: Mettur Dam in Tamil Nadu is much thicker at the bottom than at the top.
A storage tank has thicker walls at the bottom than at the top.
A tall water tank on legs has its outlet pipe at the bottom, where the push is the strongest.
explanations.art: A dam with a thick base and a thin top, and arrows of water pressure that get longer towards the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains why the walls of dams are wide at the bottom.

explanations.concept: A push on trapped liquid goes everywhere
explanations.definition: When you push on a liquid trapped in a closed pipe, the extra pressure goes to every part of the liquid equally. This is Pascal's principle.
explanations.description: Fill a tube joined to two syringes with water, with no air. Push one plunger in, and the other one moves out. Your push has travelled through the water. If the second piston is much wider than the first, the same pressure pushes on a bigger area, so the force is much bigger. A piston with 100 times the area gets 100 times the force. This is how hydraulic machines work. Car brakes, the arm of an excavator and a barber's chair all use it. There is a catch. The big piston moves much less. A 100 times bigger force means a 100 times shorter move. Nothing is gained for free.
examples: A foot pushing a brake pedal makes a strong push at the wheel.
An excavator's arm lifts tonnes of soil with a liquid pushed through tubes.
A car jack lifts a heavy car with a few pumps of a handle.
explanations.art: Two syringes joined by a tube of coloured water, a small piston on the left and a wide piston on the right.
explanations.context: This card explains how a push passes through a closed liquid, and how machines use it.

explanations.concept: Why a liquid passes on a push but a bubble does not
explanations.definition: A liquid is very nearly incompressible, so it passes on a push almost at once. Air is easy to squeeze, so a bubble of air soaks up some of the push.
explanations.description: Water particles touch, so a push on one end moves the particles all the way along the pipe. If there is a bubble of air in the pipe, the bubble gets squashed first. Part of your push goes into squeezing the air, and the other end moves less. This is why a car's brakes feel soft and spongy if air gets into the brake fluid. Mechanics get rid of the air by letting a little fluid out of each wheel. They call this bleeding the brakes. The same thing happens with the syringes of a hydraulic arm, and that is why every bubble must be tapped out before you start.
examples: A spongy brake pedal can mean that there is air in the brake fluid.
A hydraulic arm made of syringes with a bubble in the tube moves slowly and unevenly.
A medicine syringe is held upright and tapped to get the air to the top before the dose is pushed.
explanations.art: A pipe of liquid with a squashed air bubble in the middle, and a push arrow weaker on the far side of the bubble.
explanations.context: This card explains why air bubbles spoil a hydraulic machine.

explanations.concept: Pressure in the body and the deep sea
explanations.definition: Your blood is a liquid, so its pressure also depends on depth. A diver or a deep-sea animal feels a bigger and bigger push of water as she goes down.
explanations.description: When you stand, the blood in your feet is pushed down by the blood above, so the pressure in your feet is bigger than in your head. If you stand up too fast, the blood pools in your legs and you can feel dizzy. A giraffe's heart makes about twice as much blood pressure as ours, to push blood up the long neck to her head. In the sea, the push grows with every metre. At the deepest part of the ocean, about 11 kilometres down, the water pushes with more than a thousand times the push of the air at the surface. Animals that live there have bodies without air pockets to be crushed. Sperm whales dive more than a kilometre, and scientists think their lungs fold flat as they go down.
examples: Standing up quickly can make you feel dizzy for a moment.
Your ears feel the push in the deep end of a swimming pool.
A submarine's hull must be very strong to survive deep dives.
explanations.art: A diver sinking through the sea with arrows of push getting bigger, and a deep-sea fish at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains how pressure affects living bodies.

explanations.description: A siphon is a tube that empties a container over its rim. Fill the tube with water, put one end under the water in a drum and the other end lower down outside, and the water keeps running out. Everyone agrees that the outlet must be lower than the water surface in the drum, and that gravity pulls the water down the longer side. Scientists argue about the part played by the air. In the textbook version, the push of the outside air on the water surface in the drum is what pushes the water up and over. In the newer version, the water in the tube behaves like a chain, and its particles hold on to each other, so the falling side pulls the rising side along. Some experiments have reported siphons running inside a vacuum chamber, which started the argument again.
examples: A water drum can be emptied into a bucket on the floor with a siphon.
Fish tank owners siphon dirty water out of their tanks.
A siphon stops working if air gets into the tube, because the chain of water is broken.

perspectives.explanation: The push of the air on the surface of the water in the drum pushes the water up the tube and over the top. Without air pressure, the water could not rise. This is the version taught in many textbooks.

The water particles hold on to each other, so the falling water pulls the rest along, like a chain over a pulley. Some experiments reported that siphons keep running when the air is removed, which fits this view.

explanations.art: A drum with a tube going over its rim and down into a bucket, and a question mark over the top of the tube.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument among scientists: is a siphon driven by air pressure, or by the water pulling itself along?

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree about the push of water at depth.
agreed.text: The pressure in a liquid grows steadily with depth, and at one depth it is the same in every direction.
agreed.evidence: Pressure gauges lowered into lakes and oceans read bigger and bigger values with depth, and the numbers match the weight of the water above.

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree that depth, and not the amount, sets the push.
agreed.text: At a given depth, the pressure does not depend on the shape of the container or on how much water is beside it.
agreed.evidence: Vessels of many shapes and widths, filled to the same depth, give the same reading at the bottom.

agreed.context: This card is about Pascal's principle.
agreed.text: A change in pressure at one place in a closed liquid is passed on equally to every other place.
agreed.evidence: Hydraulic presses, jacks and brakes work exactly as this rule predicts.

agreed.text: Water that can flow freely settles to the same height in all connected containers.
agreed.evidence: Builders have used water levels for thousands of years, and they agree with other tools.

agreed.context: This card is about the weight of a liquid.
agreed.text: At the same depth, a denser liquid pushes harder than a lighter one, whatever its thickness.
agreed.evidence: Measurements in salt water, fresh water, oil and mercury show that pressure follows the weight of the liquid, and not how runny it is.

agreed.context: This card is about air pressure.
agreed.text: The air around us pushes on everything with about the weight of one kilogram on each square centimetre.
agreed.evidence: Barometers have measured this push since the 1640s, and it falls as you climb a mountain.

agreed.context: This card is about the deep sea.
agreed.text: The pressure at the bottom of the deepest ocean trenches is more than a thousand times the pressure at the surface, and living things are found there.
agreed.evidence: Instruments and sampling vehicles sent to the deepest trench have measured the pressure and found animals living at great depths.

challenging.context: This card is about a very common idea.
challenging.claim: A bigger amount of water pushes harder at the bottom, so a wide lake pushes harder than a thin tube.
challenging.who: Many people, for a long time before 1586
challenging.for: A lake is so heavy, and a tube of water holds so little. It seems clear that more water must push harder.
challenging.against: The push at a depth depends on the depth only. A thin tube 1 metre deep and a lake 1 metre deep push equally on each bit of the bottom. The lake pushes on a bigger area, so its total force is larger, but the pressure is the same.

challenging.context: This card is about the direction of water's push.
challenging.claim: Water only pushes downwards, because of gravity.
challenging.for: Things fall down, and water flows down.
challenging.against: Water pushes sideways on the walls of a bottle, upwards under a boat, and in every direction at once at a point. Jets leave a bottle sideways from the wall.

challenging.context: This card is about drinking through a straw.
challenging.claim: When you drink through a straw, you suck the liquid up.
challenging.for: It feels as if your mouth pulls the juice upwards.
challenging.against: When you draw in your breath, the air pressure in the straw falls. The air outside pushes down on the juice in the glass, and this push is what drives the juice up the straw. A straw with a hole in its side does not work, because air comes in through the hole.

challenging.context: This card is about thick liquids.
challenging.claim: A thick liquid pushes harder than a runny one at the same depth.
challenging.for: Honey is thick, and a jar of honey pushes harder on the bottom than a jar of water.
challenging.against: Honey pushes harder because it is heavier for its size. Coconut oil is thicker than water, but lighter, and it pushes less. Pressure depends on the weight of the liquid, not on how runny it is.

challenging.claim: Water from a tank can squirt higher than the water level in the tank.
challenging.for: A jet leaving a low hole seems to have plenty of force to go very high.
challenging.against: The jet cannot rise above the level of the water that feeds it, apart from small splashes. All the push comes from the height of that water. A fountain that goes higher needs a pump or a higher tank.

challenging.context: This card is about a very old idea from the 1600s.
challenging.claim: Nature hates empty space, so a pump can lift water to any height.
challenging.for: A pump sucks, and water follows to fill the space.
challenging.against: Well-diggers found that pumps could not lift water higher than about 10 metres. In the 1640s, Evangelista Torricelli explained this by the push of the air. The air pushes the water up, and the push is only enough to hold up a column of about 10 metres.

challenging.context: This card is about a dam wall.
challenging.claim: A dam wall can be the same thickness all the way down.
challenging.for: A wall looks strong enough if it is strong enough at the top.
challenging.against: The push of water grows with depth. At the bottom of a tall dam, it is far bigger than at the top. A wall must be much thicker there, or it would break.

big_questions.q: The water in a thin tube and the water in a huge lake push equally at the same depth. If the lake has so much more water, why isn't its push bigger?
big_questions.hint: Think about which water is actually pressing on a small spot at the bottom.

big_questions.q: A fish at the bottom of a pond has the whole pond above her. Does she feel the whole weight of the pond?
big_questions.hint: Think about the water straight above her, and the water to the sides that is held up by the pond bed.

big_questions.q: Water always settles to the same level without anybody telling it to. What does that tell you about the push inside the water?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens if one side is higher. Where does the water at the bottom get pushed?

big_questions.q: The deeper you go in the sea, the bigger the push. What stops a deep-sea fish from being crushed?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air spaces in your body, and the fluids of the fish that push back from inside.

big_questions.q: Why is the weakest tap in a building not on the ground floor but at the top?
big_questions.hint: Think about the depth of the water above each tap in the roof tank.

big_questions.q: A hydraulic machine can lift a car with a small push, but the small piston must move a long way. Is it a trick?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you give up when you get a bigger force. Does the machine give you more work, or just a different push?

big_questions.q: If you could dive to the bottom of the deepest ocean, how would the push of the water feel on your body?
big_questions.hint: Think about a weight of more than a thousand one-kilogram bags on each square centimetre, and what would happen to the air spaces in you.

big_questions.q: Scientists still argue about how a siphon works. Why might it be hard to be sure about something so ordinary?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many things happen at once in a siphon, and how hard it is to test each one by itself.

big_questions.q: Dams were built for thousands of years before anyone understood pressure. How could builders know to make them thicker at the bottom?
big_questions.hint: Think about what builders see when a dam is too thin, and what they learn from a failure.

story.title: The Tap That Sighed
story.note: A made-up story. Devika, her Ammamma, Mathew chettan, Mr Nair and the building are imagined. The science is real. A roof tank pushes water down the pipes by the depth of the water in it, and a nearly empty tank gives the taps just below it a weak push. Many other things also affect a tap, such as the width of the pipes and how many taps are open at once.
text: Devika lived at the very top of Sea Breeze Apartments in Kochi. Her flat was on the fifth floor, just under the roof. She lived there with her grandmother, who she called Ammamma.

Every morning at seven o'clock, the whole building woke up and turned on its taps. Devika's tap did not roar. It sighed. A thin thread of water crept out, and filling one bucket took as long as singing three songs.
Her friend Anoop lived on the ground floor. When he opened his tap, the water leapt out and splashed his shirt. 'Your tap is so strong,' Devika told him. 'Mine is tired.'

On Sunday there was a meeting of all the families in the hall. Everyone spoke at once. Mr Nair, the secretary, banged on the table. 'The top floors need a bigger pump,' he said. 'It will cost eighty thousand rupees.'

Mathew chettan, the caretaker, scratched his head. He was a tall, quiet man who had looked after the building for twelve years. 'The tank on the roof holds five thousand litres,' he said. 'I fill it every night. It is a very big tank. I do not understand why the fifth floor gets so little.'

Devika was sitting on the stairs outside the hall, listening through the door. That week at school she had made a science project with a bottle full of water, with three holes in its side. She remembered something strange. When the bottle was full, the jets leapt out far. When it was half empty, the jets came out weak, though there was still plenty of water inside.
'It isn't how much water there is,' she thought. 'It's how high the water stands above the hole.'
She thought about the tank on the roof. At seven in the morning, after everyone had bathed and filled their buckets, the tank must be almost empty. And her tap was only a little way below it.

The next morning Devika asked Mathew chettan to climb to the roof with her at quarter past seven. He was surprised, but he came. They lifted the lid of the big black tank. At the bottom lay a shallow pool of water, no deeper than Devika's hand.
'See?' said Mathew chettan. 'There is water. Not much, but enough to flow.'
'It flows,' said Devika, 'but it doesn't push. The push on a pipe comes from the water standing above it. A tank can be huge, but if the water is only a hand deep, the push is small.'

She pointed down at the building. 'Anoop's tap is at the very bottom, many floors below the tank. There is a tall column of water above his pipe, even when the tank is nearly empty. So it hardly changes for him. My tap is just a little below the tank. When the tank is full, there is a whole metre of water above my pipe, and it pushes well. When it is nearly empty, there is almost nothing above it.'
Mathew chettan was quiet for a while. Then he laughed. 'In twelve years, nobody has explained my own tank to me. And a girl of nine has done it in three minutes.'
'Then we need a taller tank,' he said. 'Or a bigger pump.'

'Or we keep the tank deep at seven o'clock,' said Devika. 'The pump fills it at night, and by seven it is empty. If it ran again at quarter to six, there would be a lot of water in it when everyone wakes up.'

At the next meeting, Devika brought her bottle. She held it over a bucket in front of all the families and let the water jet from the three holes. 'Look at the lowest one,' she said. 'It's the strongest, because there is the most water above it.' Then she watched the water fall to half, and the jets shrank. 'Same bottle, same holes, same water. Only the depth changed.'
Mr Nair pushed up his glasses. 'So it is not the size of the tank. It is the depth of the water.' 'Yes, uncle,' said Devika.
Mathew chettan put a small timer on the pump switch, so that the pump ran again at quarter to six every morning. It cost a few hundred rupees, and not eighty thousand.
On Monday at seven o'clock, Devika turned her tap. A strong, steady stream rushed out into the bucket. Ammamma clapped her hands.

Anoop called her on the phone. 'Is your tap better?' 'Yes,' said Devika. 'Now the tank is deep in the morning.' There was a pause. 'And mine was always strong,' said Anoop, 'because I live at the bottom of the whole building's water.'
story.epiphany: The push of water out of a tap depends on how high the water stands above the tap, and not on how much water is in the tank. A deep tank pushes harder than a shallow one, even if the shallow one is wider.
ask: Why was the tap on the ground floor strong even when the roof tank was nearly empty?
Why did the top-floor tap get weaker as the water in the roof tank went down?
Devika's bottle jets got weaker as the bottle emptied. How did that help her understand the tank?
What did the new timer change inside the roof tank at seven in the morning?
Mr Nair thought a bigger pump was the answer. Why was the problem not about how big the tank was?
