games.title: Where Is the Push Bigger? A card game about pressure
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows two places or things, A and B. You vote on where the push of the water or the pressure is bigger, and you say why.

setup.art: A table with a pile of cards and three vote tokens in front of each player, labelled A is bigger, B is bigger and Same.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the vote tokens. Give each player three tokens.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while the other players each place one token face down.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Each player places one token face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned over together and the card turned over to show the answer, with a hand giving a point.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. Check the back of the card.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: two places or things, A and B, on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A: a fish 1 metre down in a pond. B: a fish 3 metres down in the same pond. Which feels a bigger push of water?
items.b: B. It is deeper, so there is more water above.

items.f: A: the bottom of a tall thin tube of water, 1 metre deep. B: the bottom of a wide pool, also 1 metre deep. Which has the bigger push on each bit of the bottom?
items.b: Same. The push depends on the depth, and both are 1 metre deep.

items.f: A: a hole 5 centimetres below the water level in a bottle. B: a hole 15 centimetres below. Which gives the stronger jet?
items.b: B. It is deeper, so the push is bigger.

items.f: A: a tap on the ground floor. B: a tap on the fifth floor. The roof tank is the same. Which gets the bigger push of water?
items.b: A. It is much further below the water in the tank.

items.f: A: the sea 10 metres down. B: the sea 20 metres down. Which feels a bigger push?
items.b: B. The deeper you go, the bigger the push.

items.f: A: a tank that is half full. B: the same tank, full. At the tap at the bottom, which has the bigger push?
items.b: B. The water is deeper above the tap.

items.f: A: a bucket of honey 20 centimetres deep. B: a bucket of water 20 centimetres deep. Which pushes harder on the bottom?
items.b: A. Honey is heavier for its size than water.

items.f: A: coconut oil 20 centimetres deep. B: water 20 centimetres deep. Which pushes harder on the bottom?
items.b: B. Oil is thicker than water, but lighter, so it pushes less.

items.f: A: the push of water on the side wall of a tank at 1 metre down. B: the push on the bottom of the tank, also 1 metre down. Which is bigger?
items.b: Same. At one depth, the push is the same in every direction.

items.f: A: a swimmer 2 metres down in a small pool. B: a swimmer 2 metres down in a big lake. Both are fresh water. Which feels a bigger push?
items.b: Same. Only the depth matters.

items.f: A: the bottom of a dam wall. B: the top of the dam wall. Which feels a bigger push of water?
items.b: A. It is deeper, so the wall must be thicker there.

items.f: A: a small piston with an area of 1 square centimetre. B: a big piston with an area 10 times as large. The same liquid pushes on both. Which gets the bigger force?
items.b: B. The same pressure on 10 times the area gives 10 times the force.

items.f: A: a car's brake line with a bubble of air in it. B: a brake line with no air. Which gives a firm pedal?
items.b: B. Air squashes, and soaks up some of the push.

items.f: A: a tap on the first floor. B: a tap on the second floor. The roof tank is the same. Which gets the stronger push?
items.b: A. It is further below the water in the tank.

items.f: A: the water in the spout of a kettle. B: the water in the body of the kettle. Which stands higher?
items.b: Same. Water finds its own level.

items.f: A: the blood pressure in your feet when you stand. B: the blood pressure in your head when you stand. Which is bigger?
items.b: A. The blood in your legs is deeper below your heart.

items.f: A: a fish at 1,000 metres deep in the sea. B: a fish near the surface. Which feels a bigger push?
items.b: A. It has about 1,000 metres of water above it.

items.f: A: a roof tank 2 metres above a tap. B: a roof tank 6 metres above the same tap. Which gives a stronger flow?
items.b: B. More depth of water pushes on the tap.

items.f: A: a tall narrow glass of water, 15 centimetres deep. B: a wide plate with water 2 centimetres deep. Which pushes harder on its bottom?
items.b: A. It is deeper.

items.f: A: water 5 centimetres deep in a bucket. B: water 5 centimetres deep in a swimming pool. Which pushes harder on the bottom?
items.b: Same. The depth is the same.

items.f: A: a hole in the side of a bucket just under the surface. B: a hole in the side near the bottom. Which squirts farther sideways, if the bucket is on a high stool?
items.b: B. It is deeper, so the jet is stronger.

items.f: A: a diver at 10 metres. B: a diver at 30 metres. Which feels a bigger push on the body?
items.b: B. The deeper the diver, the bigger the push.

items.f: A: a pencil pressed on a board with its sharp tip. B: the same pencil pressed with its flat end, with the same force. Which makes more pressure on the board?
items.b: A. The same force is on a tiny area, so the pressure is bigger.

items.f: A: you stand on one nail. B: you lie on a bed of 500 nails. With the same weight, which pushes harder on each nail?
items.b: A. All of your weight is on one point.

printables.title: 9 vote tokens: three for each of up to three players (A is bigger, B is bigger, Same)

rules: Each player takes three vote tokens: A is bigger, B is bigger and Same. If only two play, one set is spare.
Shuffle the 24 cards and make a pile with the fronts up. One player is the reader for each card, and the job passes round.
The reader reads the front aloud. Do not turn the card over. Everyone thinks for ten seconds.
Each player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over at the same time.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer. A right token scores 1 point.
After the answer, each player with a right token must say one reason using the word depth or the word pressure. A good reason scores 1 more point.
If you were wrong, say what you will remember next time. The next reader keeps the card in a Learn pile.
When all 24 cards are played, shuffle the Learn pile and play it once more. The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone, put one token face down for each card, then check the back. Try to score at least 36 points out of a possible 48.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the nine tokens. 2. Give each player the three tokens. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, fronts up.
flow.say: Each card shows two situations, A and B. You vote on where the push is bigger. You can also vote that they are the same.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Take one of each token. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Is the Push Bigger? You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play one practice card together. Read the fish card. Do not keep the points.
flow.say: Read the card. Put your token face down. Turn them over together. Then we check the back and say why.
flow.kid: Read the fish card. Put a token down. Turn them over together.
flow.parent: This practice card scores nothing. It shows the routine: read, vote, turn over, give a reason.

check.q: A: a fish 1 metre down. B: a fish 3 metres down. Where is the push of water bigger?
options: At A
At B
The same
check.why: The deeper fish has more water above her, so she feels a bigger push. Picking A mixes up the idea of near the top with strong. Picking the same would be right only if both fish were at the same depth.

flow.do: Play twelve cards. After each card, check the back and give out the points. Put cards that were wrong in the Learn pile.
flow.say: Read the card. Vote. Turn over the tokens together. Check the back. Say a reason with depth or pressure in it.
flow.kid: Read the card. Vote. Turn over. Say a reason.

ask.q: What do the cards where the answer was the same have in common?
good: The depth was the same.
The shape or the amount of water did not matter.
Only depth matters at a point.

flow.parent: Some cards are tricky, such as the thin tube and the wide pool. Wait for the answer before saying anything.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards. Add up the points. Then shuffle the Learn pile and play it once more.
flow.say: These are the last twelve cards. Count your points when they are done. Then we replay the cards that tricked us.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points. Replay the Learn pile.
flow.parent: If the same card tricks your child twice, run the bottle test again at home with it in mind.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child think for a moment before they answer.
flow.say: Look at the cards where the answer was Same. What did the shape or the amount of water change? What did not change?
flow.kid: Which cards had the answer Same? What was the same in them?

ask.q: What do the cards with the answer Same have in common?
good: They were at the same depth.
Only the depth matters.
The shape and the amount of water did not matter.

flow.think: Can you think of two things in your house that have the same push for this reason?

experiments.title: Three Jets: how far does water squirt from holes at three heights?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three holes in a bottle at three heights, fill it with water, and measure how far each jet lands. Distances in the table are typical, not promised: your bottle, holes and stool will give different numbers, but the lowest hole should land farthest. You find out where the push of water is strongest.
experiments.question: A bottle has three holes of the same size, at three different heights. When the water squirts out, which hole sends its jet farthest, and which sends it the shortest distance?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which hole will squirt the farthest, the top one, the middle one or the bottom one? Which will squirt the shortest distance? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use one bottle, with three holes made by the same tool, so they are the same size. The water starts at the same line each time, and you keep it there by topping up from a jug. The bottle stands on the same stool each time, and you peel off all three tapes at the same moment. Only the height of the hole changes, so any difference in the jets comes from the height.
results_table: Height of the hole above the base of the bottle (cm)
Depth of the hole below the water line (cm)
Where the jet landed, measured from the foot of the stool (cm)

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle, 2 litres, with the cap taken off
a compass point (from a geometry box), a thick needle or a nail, for a grown-up to make the holes
masking tape: one strip long enough to cover all three holes (or 3 small pieces), and a marker
a stool, a chair seat or an upturned bucket about 40 centimetres high
a tape measure or long ruler, and 2 long strips of newspaper, to lay on the floor
a jug of water for filling and topping up
a bathroom, a sink or a balcony where water can run away, and a cloth to wipe the floor

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes, by pushing the compass point or nail away from the body into the bottle on a folded cloth. Keep fingers behind the point. Wet floors are slippery. Wipe up water at once. Keep water away from electric sockets and switches.
experiments.record: Fill in the table with the three results for each hole. Then draw the bottle with its three jets and show where each one landed.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results (yours will be different)

setup.art: A 2 litre bottle with three small holes in a vertical line at 4, 10 and 16 centimetres above the base, each covered by a piece of tape, and a marked water line at 22 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes three holes. Cover each with tape. Mark the water line.

setup.art: The bottle standing on a 40 centimetre stool in a bathroom, with a tape measure running along the floor from the foot of the stool and a strip of newspaper beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the bottle on the stool. Lay the tape measure on the floor.

setup.art: A child peeling three pieces of tape off at once while a second person pours water from a jug into the top of the bottle.
setup.caption: 3. Fill to the line. Peel all three tapes off at once. Keep topping up.

setup.art: Three arcs of water leaving the bottle and landing at three different spots on the strip of wet newspaper, the lowest hole landing farthest.
setup.caption: 4. Watch where each jet lands. Mark the spots.

setup.art: A child reading the distance from the tape measure at the dark wet marks on the newspaper and writing it in a table.
setup.caption: 5. Read each distance on the tape measure. Write it in the table.

flow.do: Show the bottle, the stool and the jug. Ask your child to guess, and to give a reason. Write the guess down. Do not correct it.
flow.say: We will make three holes, one high, one in the middle and one low. We fill the bottle with water. Which hole will squirt the farthest? Which will squirt the shortest distance? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three holes in a bottle. Which squirts the farthest? Why?

ask.q: Which hole will squirt the farthest, and why?
good: The top hole, because it is highest.
The bottom hole, because it has the most water above it.
The middle hole, because it is in the middle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. Write it at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the three jets test. You guess before you try.

flow.do: 1. Mark three spots in a vertical line on the bottle, at 4, 10 and 16 centimetres above the base. 2. A grown-up pushes the compass point or nail through each spot to make a hole. 3. Cover each hole with tape. 4. Mark a water line at 22 centimetres above the base.
flow.say: A grown-up will make three small holes in a straight line. Then you cover each hole with tape on the outside. Then we mark the water line.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes three holes. Cover each with tape. Mark the water line.
flow.parent: Make all three holes with the same tool, so they are the same size, about 2 millimetres. Measure the heights from the surface the bottle stands on. If the bottom of your bottle is bumpy or curved, start the lowest hole above the curve, so it does not squirt onto the bottle's own feet. If the holes are different sizes, the test is not fair. If the straight part of your bottle is shorter than 22 centimetres, put the water line 2 centimetres below where the bottle starts to narrow, and work out each depth as the water line minus the height of the hole.

flow.do: 1. Put the stool in the bathroom, or on a balcony. 2. Lay the tape measure on the floor along a straight line from the foot of the stool. 3. Stand the bottle on the edge of the stool, with the holes facing the tape measure.
flow.say: Put the stool where water can drain away. Lay the tape measure on the floor, straight out from the stool. Stand the bottle on the edge, with the holes facing the tape.
flow.kid: Put the stool in the bathroom. Lay the tape on the floor. Stand the bottle on it.
flow.parent: The stool matters. If the bottle stands on the floor, the lowest jet has no room to fall, and lands short. A 40 centimetre stool gives every jet room to fall.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle to the 22 centimetre line. 2. One person peels off the tape in one quick pull. 3. Another person pours from the jug. 4. Watch where each jet lands. Mark the wet spots. One child and a parent: the child peels and watches, the parent pours. Two to four children: one peels, one pours, one marks, one measures.
flow.say: Fill the bottle to the line. Peel all three tapes off together. Keep pouring to hold the water at the line. Watch where each jet lands.
flow.kid: Peel the tapes off together. Watch where the jets land. Mark the spots.
flow.wait: Look at the first five seconds of the jets. After that, the water level starts to fall.
flow.parent: Wet marks on the newspaper show where each jet landed. The first jets are the ones to measure; in 5 seconds the level falls only about a centimetre, so topping up is a help, not a must. Read the distance as quickly as you can. Do the test again on a dry bottle with fresh tape: tape will not stick to a wet bottle. A phone video from the side also helps.

flow.do: 1. Read each landing spot on the tape measure. 2. Write the distances in the table. 3. Dry the bottle with a cloth, put fresh tape on, refill and repeat twice more. 4. Pick the middle number for each hole.
flow.say: Read the distance for each jet. Write it in the table. Then do it two more times. Use the middle number for each hole.
flow.kid: Read the three distances. Do it twice more. Use the middle number.
flow.parent: If your results do not match, check that the holes are the same size, and that the water was kept at the line.

check.q: The lowest hole squirted the farthest. Why?
options: The water above the lowest hole is deepest, so the push is the biggest
The lowest hole is closer to the floor
The lowest hole is bigger than the others
check.why: The push of water grows with depth, because it comes from the weight of the water above. The lowest hole has the deepest water above it, so its jet leaves fastest. Picking 'closer to the floor' forgets that the jet also needs time to fall. Picking 'bigger' is wrong, because all three holes were made with the same tool.

flow.do: 1. Lower the water line by 10 centimetres, to 12 centimetres. 2. Peel off the tapes again and watch the jets. 3. Compare with the first time.
flow.say: Now we try a lower water line. Peel off the tapes again. Are the jets longer or shorter? What do you think this tells us about the water above?
flow.kid: Lower the water line. Test again. Are the jets longer or shorter?

ask.q: What happened to the jets when the water was lower, and why?
good: They were shorter, because there was less water above each hole.
They were weaker, because the push was smaller.
The push depends on the depth of the water.

flow.parent: The jets will be shorter, and the top hole will stop altogether, because it is now above the water line. Dry the bottle and use fresh tape first. Measure the distances again and add them to the table, so you can compare the two water levels with numbers.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the push of water is bigger when the water is deeper. What I saw: the lowest hole squirted the farthest, and the jets got shorter when the water was lower. Why: the push comes from the weight of the water above, and deeper holes have more water above them.
flow.think: If the bottle were twice as wide but held the same depth of water, do you think the jets would be longer, shorter or the same? Why?

experiments.title: Same Level: mark a level line on a wall with a hose
experiments.context: In this experiment you fill a clear hose with coloured water, and use it to mark two spots on a wall 3 metres apart. You find out if the marks are at the same height, and how a wide funnel and an air bubble change the result.
experiments.question: A clear hose full of water has one end at each of two spots on a wall, 3 metres apart. The water in the hose stands at some height at each end. Are the two heights the same? Does a wide funnel on one end change it? Does a bubble of air?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the two marks be at the same height from the floor? Will the water stand higher in the wide funnel or in the thin end of the hose? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use the same hose, filled with the same coloured water, for every test. The two ends are held against the same wall, 3 metres apart, and you wait for the water to stop moving before you mark it. You measure the height of each mark from the floor in the same way. Only one thing changes in each test: a plain end, a funnel on one end, or a bubble in the hose.

materials.item: a clear plastic hose about 4 metres long, with an inside width of 6 to 10 millimetres (a plumber's or hardware shop 'water level' pipe; if it costs too much, 3 metres works with the marks 2 metres apart)
a bucket or large bowl of water, with a few drops of food colour, or a pinch of haldi or a drop of ink, so you can see the water
a kitchen funnel, wide at the top, with a stem that fits into the hose (push the hose on, or tape it)
masking tape, and a pencil, to mark the wall
a tape measure, and a ruler
a helper to hold the other end of the hose (or a second end taped to the wall at a fixed height)
a long wall with a flat floor, and a cloth to mop up spills

experiments.safety: Keep water away from electric sockets and switches. Wipe up spills at once, because wet floors are slippery. Do not suck the hose to fill it. Fill it by dipping it in the bucket. Do not drink the coloured water. Skip food colour if anyone at home is allergic to it, and note that haldi and ink stain clothes.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three tests. Then draw the wall, the hose, and the two marks, and write the height of each mark.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results (typical, yours will be different)

setup.art: A clear hose being pushed under the coloured water in a bucket, until no bubbles come out of either end, with a child pinching both ends with thumbs.
setup.caption: 1. Dip the whole hose in coloured water. Keep both ends shut with your thumbs.

setup.art: Two children each holding one end of the hose upright against a wall, 3 metres apart, with the water standing in the top of each end.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the two ends against the wall, 3 metres apart. Wait for the water to stop.

setup.art: A child marking the water level at one end of the hose on a piece of masking tape on the wall, with a pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the water level at each end with tape and a pencil.

setup.art: A child measuring the height of the two marks from the floor with a tape measure, and writing the numbers in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the height of each mark from the floor.

setup.art: A kitchen funnel on one end of the hose, with the water standing at the same height in the funnel and the thin end.
setup.caption: 5. Try a funnel on one end. Compare the water level in both ends.

flow.do: Show the hose, the funnel and the wall. Ask your child to guess, and to give a reason. Write the guess down. Do not correct it.
flow.say: We will fill a long hose with water and use it to mark two spots on a wall, 3 metres apart. Will the two marks be at the same height? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A hose full of water. Two marks, 3 metres apart. Same height? Why?

ask.q: Will the two marks be at the same height from the floor, and why?
good: Yes, because the water in the hose stays level.
No, because the water will run to one end.
Yes, because both ends are open to the air.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of the level line test. You guess before you try.

flow.do: 1. Put a few drops of food colour in the bucket of water. 2. Push the whole hose under the water. 3. Hold it there until no bubbles come out of either end. 4. Pinch both ends with your thumbs and lift the hose out.
flow.say: Push the whole hose under the coloured water. Wait until no more bubbles come out. Keep both ends shut with your thumbs. Then lift it out.
flow.kid: Push the whole hose under the water. Wait for no more bubbles.
flow.parent: Look along the hose against the light. Any bubble you can see will spoil the test. If there is a bubble, put the hose back under the water and try again. A hose that is too thin (under 6 millimetres) holds bubbles stubbornly. Coil the hose in the bucket, and wriggle it so bubbles rise out.

flow.do: 1. Hold both ends at the same height, with the middle hanging low. 2. Each person holds one end of the hose upright against the wall, 3 metres apart. 3. Lift or lower the ends until the water stands a few centimetres below the top of the hose at each end. 4. Wait until the water stops moving. 5. Mark the water level on a piece of tape on the wall at each end.
flow.say: Each of you holds one end against the wall. Move the ends up or down until the water stands near the top of each one. Wait for it to settle. Then mark the wall at the water.
flow.kid: Hold the hose ends against the wall. Wait for the water to settle. Mark it.
flow.wait: The water may bob up and down for a few seconds. Wait until it is still.
flow.parent: Keep the ends of the hose upright, and keep the middle low. If the water runs out, lift your ends higher. One child on their own can tape one end to the wall and hold the other. With 2 to 4 children, two hold the ends, one marks and one measures, and then swap.

flow.do: 1. Measure the height of each mark from the floor with the tape measure. 2. Write the numbers in the table. 3. Work out the difference. 4. Ask your child what they notice.
flow.say: Measure each mark from the floor. Write the heights in the table. Are they the same? How close are they?
flow.kid: Measure each mark from the floor. Are they the same height?
flow.parent: A small difference of a few millimetres is normal. If the difference is big, check for a bubble. If the floor is uneven, the marks can be level while their heights from the floor are not the same.

check.q: The two marks, 3 metres apart, are the same height from the floor. Why?
options: The water in the hose settles at the same level at both ends
The wall is the same colour
The hose is longer than the wall
check.why: Water that can flow freely settles to the same level everywhere it is joined. So the water at both ends stands at the same height. Picking the other answers means looking at things that have no link to the water level.

flow.do: 1. Fit the funnel on one end of the hose. 2. Pour a little coloured water into the funnel until it is part full. 3. Wait for the water to settle. 4. Compare the water level in the funnel with the level in the thin end, using the ruler.
flow.say: Put the wide funnel on one end. Pour in a little more water. Is the water higher in the wide funnel or in the thin end? Measure it.
flow.kid: Put the funnel on one end. Compare the two water levels.

ask.q: Is the water higher in the wide funnel or in the thin end, and why?
good: The same, because only the depth matters.
Higher in the wide funnel, because there is more water.
The same, because water finds its own level.

flow.parent: Many people guess that the wide funnel pushes harder because it holds more water. The levels will be nearly the same, within a few millimetres.

flow.do: 1. Let a bubble about 5 centimetres long into the hose. 2. Slide it into the upright part, near one end. 3. Mark both ends again. 4. Measure the heights and write the difference in the table.
flow.say: Now we let a bubble into the hose and slide it into the upright part, near one end. Mark the wall again at both ends. Are the two marks still at the same height?
flow.kid: Let a bubble into the hose. Mark again. Are the marks still level?
flow.parent: Air weighs almost nothing, so the bubble holds up no water. The water on the bubble side has to stand higher, by about the length of the bubble that sits in the upright part, which is about 5 centimetres. A bubble lying in the low, flat part of the hose does almost nothing. That is why masons check their hoses for bubbles.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water in joined containers settles at the same level, whatever their width. What I saw: the two marks were within a few millimetres, the funnel made no difference, and the bubble spoiled it. Why: water at the same depth has the same push, so if one side were higher it would be pushed down until the push was equal.
flow.think: How could a mason use this hose to check that the tops of two walls in a house are at the same height?

activities.title: Tap Survey: which tap fills a litre the fastest?
activities.context: In this activity you time how long each tap in your home takes to fill a one-litre bottle. You look for a pattern, and ask what else, besides the push of the water, could change the speed.

materials.item: a 1 litre bottle or measuring jug (a bottle with a wide mouth catches the water best)
a stopwatch or a phone timer
a bucket, to catch and reuse the water for plants
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler for the table

activities.safety: Use cold water only. Do not time a hot tap, a geyser or a hot shower, because hot water can scald. Wipe up spills at once, because wet floors are slippery.

schedule.what: Guess which tap is fastest. Time each tap filling one litre. Put the taps in order and look for a reason.

activities.record: A table with each tap's name, where it is, your guess in order, the time in seconds to fill one litre, and the real order.

setup.art: A kitchen tap running into a one litre bottle, with a child holding a phone timer.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the bottle under the tap, fully open. Start the timer.

setup.art: A child writing the name and time of each tap in a table, with a bathroom basin tap, a bucket tap and a shower in the background.
setup.caption: 2. Time each tap in the house. Write the times in a table.

setup.art: A row of cards with tap names put in order from fastest to slowest.
setup.caption: 3. Put the taps in order from the fastest to the slowest.

flow.do: Walk round the home with your child and list the taps. Ask for a guess about which will be fastest and which will be slowest. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Let's find all the taps in our home. Which will fill a litre bottle the fastest? Which will be the slowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: List every tap. Which will be the fastest? Which the slowest? Why?

ask.q: Which tap do you think is fastest, and why?
good: The bucket tap, because the pipe is wide.
The kitchen tap, because it is the strongest.
The tap that is lowest, because there is more water above it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Count taps in the bathroom, kitchen, balcony, and any outside tap.
flow.context: This is the first step of the tap survey. You list the taps and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Open the tap fully. 2. Hold the bottle under it and start the timer. 3. Stop when the bottle is full. 4. Write the time. 5. Pour the water into the bucket. 6. Do the same for each tap.
flow.say: Open the tap fully. Start the timer when the bottle goes under. Stop when it is full. Write the time. Do all the taps. Keep the water in the bucket.
flow.kid: Open the tap fully. Time one litre. Write it down. Try every tap.
flow.parent: Close all the other taps first, so the same push is not shared with other taps. Time each tap twice and use the middle number if you can. Use the bucket of water for plants. Roles for 2 to 4 children: one holds the bottle, one times, one writes, and then swap so each child times one tap. One child alone: the parent holds the bottle while the child times and writes.

flow.do: 1. Put the taps in order from the fastest to the slowest. 2. Mark which are on the highest and lowest floor of your home, or nearest to the tank. 3. Work out litres per minute for each tap: 60 divided by the seconds. 4. Look for a pattern.
flow.say: Put the taps in order. Which was the fastest? Which was the slowest? Where is each one in the house? Do you see a pattern?
flow.kid: Put the taps in order. Where are they in the house? Do you see a pattern?
flow.parent: Many things besides the push change the speed. The width of the pipe, the tap's design and other taps open at the same time all matter. Do not worry if there is no clear pattern. Times such as 10 to 40 seconds are typical, but yours may differ because of your pipes, your pump and what else is running. In a one-floor flat, compare tap types instead, or time the same tap at a busy time (morning) and a quiet time (afternoon), and ask if the pattern holds.

check.q: The tap closest below the roof tank filled the bottle the slowest. What could explain this?
options: There is less depth of water above it pushing it than above a lower tap
It is the oldest tap
Water cannot go uphill
check.why: A tap close below the tank has only a small depth of water above it, so the push is smaller. Picking 'oldest' could be partly true for other reasons, but it does not link to the push. Water going 'uphill' is not the issue, as the tap is below the tank.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Was this a fair test? What would we need to change to make it fairer?
flow.kid: Was this a fair test? What would make it fairer?
flow.think: Name two things, besides the height of the tap, that could change how fast it fills a bottle.

activities.title: Four Holes, One Squeeze: does a push spread through water?
activities.context: In this activity you fill a bottle with water, with four holes in a ring at one height. You squeeze the bottle, and you watch what the four jets do.

materials.item: a plastic bottle of 500 millilitres with a tight cap, with thin sides that can be squeezed (a packaged-water bottle works well)
a compass point or thick needle (a thin pin makes holes too small), for a grown-up to make the holes
4 small pieces of masking tape
a jug of water
a sink or a bathroom floor where water can run away, and a towel
a sheet of newspaper or a tray to catch the jets

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the holes, by pushing the compass point or needle away from the body into the bottle on a folded cloth. Wet floors are slippery. Wipe up spills at once.

schedule.what: Make four holes in a ring. Fill the bottle to the brim. Squeeze it and watch the four jets.

activities.record: Draw the bottle from above, with the four jets as arrows. Write if the four jets were the same or different.

setup.art: A bottle with four small holes in a ring around its middle, each covered with a piece of tape.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes four holes in a ring, at the same height. Cover each with tape.

setup.art: A bottle filled to the very brim, with its cap screwed on tight, held over a sink.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the bottle to the brim. Close the cap tight.

setup.art: A child squeezing the bottle with both hands, and four jets of water shooting out in four directions.
setup.caption: 3. Peel off the tapes. Squeeze the bottle gently.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes four holes in a ring around the bottle, 5 centimetres above the base. 2. Cover each hole with a piece of tape. 3. Ask your child to guess what will happen when the bottle is squeezed.
flow.say: Four holes, all at the same height. When we squeeze the bottle, what will the four jets do? Will they be the same or different? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up makes four holes. When you squeeze, what will the jets do? Why?

ask.q: What do you think the four jets will do, and why?
good: They will be the same, because the holes are the same.
The jet nearest my hand will be strongest.
Only the jet on the other side will come out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Make the four holes the same size.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Holes, One Squeeze. A grown-up makes the holes, and you guess.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle to the very top with water. 2. Screw the cap on tight. 3. Hold it over the sink. 4. Peel off the four tapes.
flow.say: Fill the bottle to the very top, so there is no air. Close the cap tight. Hold it over the sink. Peel off the tapes. What happens?
flow.kid: Fill to the brim. Close the cap. Peel off the tapes. What happens?
flow.parent: With the cap on tight and the bottle full to the brim, the water stays inside, because the water cannot get out without letting air in. A few drops may come out. That is normal. If water pours out with the cap on, the holes are too big: use a thinner needle on a new bottle. If nothing squirts when you squeeze in the next step, the cap is loose or there is air in the bottle.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze the sides of the bottle gently with both hands. 2. Watch the four jets. 3. Squeeze the bottle from a different side and watch again. 4. Put the bottle on the newspaper, squeeze once gently and once harder, and mark how far each jet lands each time. 5. Let go, and watch the holes.
flow.say: Squeeze the bottle gently. What do the four jets do? Squeeze from a different side. Are the jets the same? What happens when you let go?
flow.kid: Squeeze the bottle. Watch the four jets. Squeeze from another side.

ask.q: What did the four jets do when you squeezed?
good: They all shot out at the same time.
They were about the same strength.
They came out straight, away from the wall.

flow.parent: The four jets come out together, about equally strong, and straight out from the wall, whichever side you squeeze. A harder squeeze makes all four jets longer by about the same amount. When you let go, air bubbles are drawn in through the holes. One child can squeeze while another marks the landing spots; with one child and a parent, the parent marks. Squeeze over a sink or tray, because wet floors are slippery.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Your hand squeezed one side. Why did the water shoot out of all four holes?
flow.kid: You squeezed one side. Why did all four jets shoot out?

check.q: You squeezed one side of the bottle, and the water shot out of four holes at once. What does this show?
options: A push on a trapped liquid goes to every part of it
Water likes to go round corners
The holes are all the same size
check.why: The push you made on the water did not stay where your hand was. It travelled through the water to every hole. This is the rule that hydraulic machines use. The holes are the same size, but that does not explain why they all squirted at once.

flow.think: Where else have you seen a push travel through a liquid? Think of a brake, or a syringe.

activities.title: Draw the Push: arrows on a dam wall
activities.context: In this activity you draw a dam wall with water behind it, and draw arrows to show the push of the water at different depths. Then you design the wall.

materials.item: 2 sheets of plain paper and a ruler
a pencil, and coloured pencils or crayons
a phone or a book with pictures of a dam, such as Mettur Dam or Bhakra Nangal (a school atlas or textbook works too)
your results from the three jets test, if you have done it

schedule.what: Look at pictures of dams. Draw the push of the water as arrows. Design a wall that holds it.

activities.record: A drawing of a dam from the side, with arrows of push at five depths and a wall that is thicker at the bottom.

setup.art: A phone showing a photo of a dam wide at the bottom and narrower at the top, held next to a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Look at pictures of dams. See how the wall is shaped.

setup.art: A side view of a wall with water on one side and arrows at five depths, the arrows longer at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Draw five arrows at five depths. Make the lower ones longer.

setup.art: The same drawing with a thick wall drawn that is wider at the bottom than at the top.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a wall that is thick enough at every depth.

flow.do: Look at pictures of two or three dams. Ask your child what they notice about the shape of the wall.
flow.say: Look at these dams. What do you notice about the shape of the wall? Is it the same width at the top and at the bottom?
flow.kid: Look at the dams. What do you notice about the wall's shape?

ask.q: What do you notice about the shape of a dam wall?
good: It is wider at the bottom.
It gets thinner towards the top.
It is thickest where the water is deepest.

flow.parent: Look for pictures of Mettur Dam in Tamil Nadu, Bhakra Dam in Himachal Pradesh and Tehri Dam in Uttarakhand.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Push. You look at real dams and notice their shape.

flow.do: 1. Draw a tall wall on the right side of the paper. 2. Draw water on the left, up to near the top. 3. Mark five depths on the wall, 2 centimetres apart. 4. Draw an arrow at each depth. 5. Make the top arrow 1 centimetre long, and each one below 1 centimetre longer. 6. Check with the ruler: the arrow at 10 centimetres depth is five times the arrow at 2 centimetres.
flow.say: Draw the water and the wall. Mark five depths. At each depth, draw an arrow pushing on the wall. The deeper the depth, the longer the arrow.
flow.kid: Draw the wall and the water. Draw five arrows. Deeper means longer.
flow.parent: The arrows should get longer in even steps, because the push grows evenly with depth. The top arrow is the shortest. Ask your child to predict the length of the bottom arrow before drawing it, then check. With 2 to 4 children, each draws their own dam and then compares which arrow lengths match.

flow.do: 1. Draw a thick wall that is strong enough at each depth. 2. Make it thin at the top and thick at the bottom. 3. Label the thickest and thinnest places.
flow.say: Now draw the wall. Where does it need to be thickest? Where can it be thinner? Label them.
flow.kid: Draw the wall. Make it thickest where the push is biggest.

check.q: Where does a dam wall need to be the thickest?
options: At the bottom, where the water is deepest and the push is the biggest
At the top, where it is highest
Everywhere the same
check.why: The push of the water is biggest at the bottom, so the wall must be strongest there. Picking the top mixes up high with strong. Picking the same everywhere would waste material at the top and risk breaking at the bottom.

flow.do: Ask your child to show the drawing to someone and explain it.
flow.say: Show your drawing to someone. Explain why the arrows are different lengths and why the wall is the shape it is.
flow.kid: Show your drawing. Explain why the wall is thickest at the bottom.
flow.think: Why do you think builders of dams a thousand years ago still made them thicker at the bottom?

activities.title: Straw Trouble: is drinking sucking or pushing?
activities.context: In this activity you drink through a straw, then through a straw with a hole in it, and then through a straw in a sealed bottle. You find out what really lifts the drink up the straw.

materials.item: 3 straws for each child, thin ones from a juice box are fine (paper straws go soggy)
a glass of water or juice
a pin or a needle, for a grown-up to make a hole about 2 millimetres wide
a small, stiff bottle with a narrow mouth (a cold-drink bottle, not a thin water bottle that will crumple), and a lump of modelling clay or soft atta dough
a cloth to mop spills

activities.safety: A grown-up uses the pin or needle, and pushes it away from the body. Keep straws and clay away from children under five. Never blow into the sealed bottle. Use plain water, or a drink that nobody at home is allergic to. Do not eat the clay. Each child uses their own straw, never a shared one.

schedule.what: Drink through a plain straw. Then through a straw with a hole. Then through a straw in a sealed bottle. Explain what you find.

activities.record: Draw the three straws, and write if you could drink or not through each one.

setup.art: A child drinking through a plain straw from a glass of juice.
setup.caption: 1. Drink through a plain straw. It works.

setup.art: A straw with a small hole near the top, in a glass of juice, and a child trying to drink.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up makes a hole near the top of a straw. Try to drink.

setup.art: A bottle with a straw pushed through a lump of clay at its mouth, with the clay sealing the mouth.
setup.caption: 3. Seal the mouth of a bottle with clay around a straw. Try to drink.

flow.do: Give your child a plain straw and a glass of water. Ask for a guess about what will happen with a hole in the straw, and for a reason.
flow.say: Drink through a plain straw. It works. Now we will put a hole in a straw. Will you still be able to drink? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Drink with a plain straw. Will a straw with a hole work? Why?

ask.q: Will a straw with a hole in it work, and why?
good: No, because air will come in through the hole.
Yes, because the hole is tiny.
No, because the water will leak out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of Straw Trouble. You guess before you try.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pricks a hole, about 2 millimetres wide, through one side of a straw, near the top, with the pin. 2. Put the straw in the glass. 3. Try to drink. 4. Cover the hole with a finger and try again.
flow.say: A grown-up will make a small hole near the top of this straw. Try to drink. Now cover the hole with your finger and try again. What changes?
flow.kid: Try to drink through the straw with a hole. Then cover the hole.
flow.parent: A tiny pinprick may still let you drink, so make a hole you can see, and place it above the drink. With the hole open, you will get a little or no drink. With the hole covered, the straw works again.

flow.do: 1. Press a thick ring of clay round the mouth of the small bottle. 2. Push a straw through the clay into the bottle. 3. Make sure there is no gap in the clay. 4. Try to drink from the bottle.
flow.say: Seal the mouth of the bottle with clay around the straw. Now try to drink the water. What happens?
flow.kid: Seal the bottle with clay. Try to drink through the straw.
flow.parent: In the sealed bottle you cannot drink after the first tiny sip, and a thin bottle will crumple inwards. If you can still drink, there is a gap in the clay: press it again. because the air cannot push on the water. In the open glass, the air pushes. This is why the straw with a hole does not work either.

check.q: When you drink through a straw, what pushes the drink up?
options: The air pressure outside pushes down on the drink in the glass
Your mouth pulls the drink up like a rope
The straw makes the water lighter
check.why: Drawing in your breath lowers the pressure inside the straw. The air outside is pushing on the surface of the drink, and this push drives the drink up the straw. Picking 'pulls like a rope' is how it feels, but the experiment with the sealed bottle shows it cannot be right. Picking 'lighter' is not true.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Drinking feels like sucking. What is really happening to the drink? Who is doing the pushing?
flow.kid: What is really happening when you drink through a straw?
flow.think: If you had a very long straw, do you think you could drink from a glass on the floor while standing on a roof? Why or why not?

projects.title: The Syringe Arm: a robot arm worked by water
projects.context: In this project you join syringes with tubes of water, and use them to move a cardboard arm. You find out how a push travels through water to move something far away.

materials.item: 4 plastic syringes of 10 millilitres (Rs 5 to 10 each at a medical shop), with no needle
2 pieces of thin, soft clear aquarium air tube about 40 centimetres long, that stretch snugly over the tips of the syringes
a bowl of coloured water, made with a few drops of food colour
a piece of strong cardboard (from a carton) and ice-cream sticks for the arm
masking tape, glue, and paper fasteners or short pieces of straw

projects.safety: Use only syringes with no needle. If a shop gives a needle, a grown-up takes it off and puts it away safely, and children never touch needles. Never point a syringe at a face. Do not drink the coloured water. A grown-up cuts the cardboard if it is thick. Keep small parts away from children under five.

schedule.what: Fill two syringes joined by a tube with water, with no air. Test that a push on one moves the other.
Build the cardboard arm. Fix a syringe pair to a joint. Test it and improve it.

projects.record: A drawing of the arm with its syringes and tubes, and a note of what you changed.

setup.art: Two syringes joined by a clear tube full of coloured water, one plunger pushed in and the other pushed out.
setup.caption: 1. Join two syringes with a tube of water. Push one plunger.

setup.art: A cardboard arm with a hinge in the middle, with two syringes joined by a tube, one fixed to the arm and one fixed to the base.
setup.caption: 2. Fix the syringes to the arm so that one plunger pushes it up.

setup.art: The arm lifting a paper cup on a string when a child pushes the plunger on the other syringe.
setup.caption: 3. Push the plunger. Lift a paper cup.

flow.do: Show your child the syringes and the tube. Ask what will happen if the two syringes are joined with water between them, and one plunger is pushed.
flow.say: Two syringes, joined by a tube of water. If I push one plunger in, what will the other plunger do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two syringes joined by water. Push one. What happens to the other? Why?

ask.q: What will the other plunger do, and why?
good: It will move out, because the water is pushed along.
It will not move, because the tube is too long.
It will move in, because it is pulled.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Syringe Arm. You guess before you build.

flow.do: 1. Put the two syringes, the tube and the bowl of coloured water together. 2. Under the water, pull water into a syringe, tap it and push out the air. 3. Still under the water, join the tube to it. 4. Fill the other syringe under the water and join it to the other end. 5. Set both plungers at about the 5 millilitre mark, so each can move in or out. 6. Push one plunger in by 2 centimetres and measure how far the other moves out.
flow.say: Fill both syringes and the tube with water, with no air at all. Tap out every bubble. Push one plunger in. What does the other one do? Push it again, a little at a time.
flow.kid: Fill both syringes and the tube. Tap out the bubbles. Push one plunger.
flow.wait: This takes a few tries. A tiny bubble makes the plunger feel spongy. Typically the other plunger moves out about the same 2 centimetres, and less if there is a bubble.
flow.parent: Draw the water in with the syringe tip under the water, so air does not enter. If the plunger feels spongy, take the tube off and fill again. Make a second pair the same way, so the arm has a control pair and an arm pair. With 2 to 4 children, each pair of children makes one pair of syringes.

check.q: A bubble of air in the tube made the other plunger move less than the first. Why?
options: The bubble was squashed, which soaked up some of the push
The bubble made the water heavier
The tube was too thin
check.why: Air is easy to squeeze, so a bubble takes in some of the push that should have gone to the far plunger. Water cannot be squeezed, so with no bubble the push is passed straight along. A bubble does not make the water heavier, and the thin tube is not the reason.

flow.do: 1. Cut two arm pieces from cardboard, each about 15 centimetres long. 2. Join them with a paper fastener to make a hinge. 3. Fix one syringe to the base and one to the arm, so that pushing the first plunger makes the arm lift. 4. Tape the syringes in place.
flow.say: Make an arm with a hinge. Fix one syringe to the base and the other to the arm, so that when the plunger is pushed, the arm moves. Use tape to hold them.
flow.kid: Build an arm with a hinge. Fix the syringes with tape.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the thick cardboard. A glue gun is not needed: masking tape, rubber bands and clay hold the syringes. There are many ways to fix the syringes. Let your child try different ones.

flow.do: 1. Push the plunger of the control syringe slowly. 2. Watch the arm lift. 3. Try lifting a light paper cup on a string. 4. Change one thing, such as the place where the syringe is fixed, and test again.
flow.say: Push the plunger slowly. Watch the arm. Can it lift a paper cup? Change one thing and try again. Does the arm move more, or less?
flow.kid: Push the plunger. Lift a cup. Change one thing and try again.

ask.q: What did you change, and what happened?
good: I moved the syringe closer to the hinge, and the arm moved more.
I used a bigger syringe, and the arm lifted more.
I took out a bubble, and the arm moved smoothly.

flow.parent: Fixing the syringe close to the hinge makes the arm swing wider but with less force. Fixing it far from the hinge gives more force but a smaller swing. This is a trade-off.
flow.think: If you used a big syringe on the arm and a small one for the control, would you need to push harder or less hard?

challenges.title: The Farthest Squirt
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You use one bottle and one hole to make a jet of water that lands as far away as you can.
challenges.problem: You have one 2 litre bottle with the cap off, and you may make one hole in it. Make the jet land as far from the bottle as possible. You may choose the height of the hole, the depth of the water, the height of the bottle above the floor, and a tilted straw in the hole (the hole is then about 6 millimetres wide, to fit the straw).
constraints: Use only one hole, about 2 millimetres wide, made by a grown-up. For the straw design, a grown-up widens the hole to fit the straw, about 6 millimetres.
Fill to the same line each try. Read where the jet lands in the first 3 seconds, while a helper tops up from a jug.
Measure the distance from the foot of the stool, along the floor, to where the jet lands.
Try each design three times and use the middle number.
materials: a 2 litre bottle with the cap off
a compass point or thick needle, for a grown-up
a stool or upturned bucket, a table edge and a pile of books
a tape measure and strips of newspaper
a jug of water, masking tape, and a bent straw with modelling clay or atta dough
challenges.safety: A grown-up makes the hole, pushing the compass point or needle away from the body into the bottle on a folded cloth. Keep fingers behind the point. Keep the bottle steady on the edge of a table, away from the floor edge. Wipe up spills at once, because wet floors are slippery.
general: Put the bottle on a higher stool, so the jet has further to fall.
Fill the bottle to the top, so the water is deeper above the hole.
Make the hole low in the bottle, where the push is strong.
creative: Push a short bent straw into a widened hole with clay or dough around it, and bend the straw upwards at an angle of about 45 degrees. A jet angled upwards usually goes farther than a flat jet, but check with your tape measure.
Put the bottle on the edge of a table, and let the jet fall to the floor, which is farther down than a stool.
Make the hole in the middle of the bottle instead of near the bottom, and compare. Does the answer change if the stool is low?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own design. Draw it, build it, measure it and show it. Which design went the farthest? Why do you think it worked best?

setup.art: A bottle on a high table with a hole near the bottom and a bent straw in the hole pointing upwards, and a long jet arching to the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Make a hole. Fit a bent straw if you like.

setup.art: A tape measure along the floor and a jug topping up the bottle while the jet lands on a strip of newspaper.
setup.caption: 2. Fill to the line. Top up from a jug. Mark where the jet lands.

setup.art: A child writing the distance for each design in a table next to a sketch of the bottle.
setup.caption: 3. Try each design three times. Write the middle number.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs, and to say which one they think will go farthest and why.
flow.say: You have one bottle and one hole. How could you make the jet go as far as possible? Sketch two ideas first. Which one do you think will win? Why?
flow.kid: Sketch two designs. Which will go farthest? Why?

ask.q: What would make a jet go farther?
good: More water above the hole.
A higher stool for the jet to fall from.
A hole at the right height.

flow.parent: Do not correct the sketches. Any plan with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Farthest Squirt challenge. You plan.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes the hole for the first design. 2. Fill the bottle to the line. 3. Top up from the jug. 4. Mark where the jet lands and read the distance. 5. Do it three times and write the middle number.
flow.say: Build your first design. Fill to the line, and keep topping up. Mark where the jet lands. Do it three times. Write the middle number. This is the number to beat.
flow.kid: Build your first design. Test it three times. Write the middle number.
flow.parent: The first number is the one to beat. Write it large. With one child, the parent pours and the child reads the landing spot. With 2 to 4 children, each invents one design and they take turns pouring, marking and recording. The bigger straw hole drains the bottle quickly, so fill high and measure early.

flow.do: 1. Change one thing in your design, such as the height of the stool or the angle of the straw. 2. Test it three times. 3. Write the middle number. 4. Keep the best design.
flow.say: Change one thing. Test it three times. Is it better or worse? Keep the best design, and try changing something else.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test it. Is it better? Keep the best.

check.q: Raising the bottle onto a higher stool made the jet land farther. Why?
options: The jet had more time to fall before it hit the floor
The push of the water was stronger
The hole was bigger
check.why: The jet leaves the hole at the same speed, but it has more time in the air before it hits the floor. So it travels farther. The push of the water depends on the depth above the hole, and that did not change. The hole is the same size.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell you what made the biggest difference.
flow.say: Which change helped the most? Why do you think it helped?
flow.kid: Which change helped the most? Why?
flow.think: If you wanted to squirt water as far as you could from a tall building, would you rather have a hole near the bottom of the tank, or near the top? Why?
