quiz.p: What does the push of water at a point depend on?
opts: How much water is in the container
quiz.why: The push comes from the water straight above the point, so it depends on the depth only. The width and the amount of water do not change it.

quiz.p: A boy dives deeper and deeper in a pool, and his ears start to hurt. Why?
opts: The push of the water on his ears gets bigger with depth
quiz.why: There is more water above him at greater depth, so it pushes harder on his ears.

quiz.p: The water in the spout of a kettle and the water in its body stand at which heights?
quiz.why: Water in joined containers settles at the same level, whatever their shapes.

quiz.p: A closed pipe is full of liquid. You push on a piston at one end. What happens?
opts: The push goes to every part of the liquid
The push stays at the piston
quiz.why: A push on a trapped liquid is passed on equally to every part of it. This is why hydraulic machines work.

quiz.p: Why is the hull of a deep-diving submarine very thick?
opts: The push of the water is huge at great depth
quiz.why: The deeper the submarine goes, the bigger the push on the hull. The hull must be strong not to be crushed.

quiz.p: A bubble of air in a hydraulic pipe makes the machine move in a spongy way. Why?
opts: Air is squashed and takes up some of the push
quiz.why: Air is easy to squeeze, so a bubble absorbs some of the push. Liquids pass on a push because they are hard to squeeze.

quiz.p: A fish just under the surface feels the same push as a fish at the bottom of a deep lake.
quiz.why: False. The fish at the bottom has far more water above her, so she feels a much bigger push.

quiz.p: Which of these will make a roof tank give a stronger push to the taps below?
opts: Making the water deeper above the taps
quiz.why: The push at a tap comes from the depth of the water above it. Colour does nothing, and a longer pipe usually slows the flow.

quiz.p: When you drink through a straw, what pushes the drink up the straw?
opts: The air pressure on the drink in the glass
Your mouth, which pulls like a rope
quiz.why: Drawing in your breath lowers the pressure in the straw. The air pushing on the drink in the glass is what drives it up.

quiz.p: A dam wall is built the same thickness all the way down.
quiz.why: False. The push grows with depth, so the wall is thickest at the bottom.

quiz.p: Which pushes harder on the bottom of a jar at the same depth, honey or coconut oil?
opts: Honey, because it is heavier for its size
Coconut oil, because it is thicker
quiz.why: Pressure follows the weight of the liquid. Honey is denser than water, and coconut oil is lighter than water.

quiz.p: A big piston has 10 times the area of a small piston, and the two are joined by a liquid. What do you gain and what do you lose?
opts: Ten times the force, but the big piston moves one tenth as far
Ten times the force and ten times the distance
The same force but more distance
quiz.why: The same pressure on a bigger area gives a bigger force. But the same amount of liquid moves the big piston a shorter way.

items.p: What does the word pressure mean?
opts: How hard something pushes on each small part of a surface
items.why: Pressure is the push on each small bit of a surface. The same weight on a smaller area makes a bigger pressure. Picking 'how heavy' leaves out the area that the push is spread over.

items.p: A swimmer swims from 1 metre deep to 3 metres deep. What happens to the push of the water on her?
items.why: There is more water above her at 3 metres, so the push is bigger. The deeper you go, the bigger the push.

items.p: Where does the push of water at a depth come from?
opts: The weight of the water above it
items.why: Gravity pulls on the water above a point, and the water below has to hold it up. That is the push. Colour and wind do not change it.

items.p: A clear hose full of water has its two ends held against a wall, 3 metres apart. What do you expect about the water in the two ends?
opts: It stands at the same height in both ends
It stands higher in the end held lower
It stands higher in the end that is wider
items.why: Water that can flow freely settles to the same level everywhere it is joined. If one end were higher, the push would move water until they were equal.

items.p: Why is a dam wall thicker at the bottom than at the top?
opts: The push of the water is biggest at the bottom
It is easier to build that way
There is less water at the bottom
items.why: The push grows with depth, so the bottom of the wall feels the biggest push and must be the strongest. There is more water above the bottom, not less.

items.p: Two syringes are joined by a tube of water. Why must there be no air in the tube?
opts: Air squashes and soaks up some of the push
items.why: Water cannot be squeezed, so it passes the push along. A bubble of air gets squashed, and the far plunger moves less.

items.p: Water pushes only downwards.
items.why: False. Water pushes on every surface it touches, sideways on a wall, upwards under a boat and downwards on a bottom.

items.p: A tall thin tube of water and a wide tank of water, both 2 metres deep, push equally on each bit of the bottom.
items.why: True. The push at a depth depends only on how deep it is. The tank pushes on a bigger area, but each bit feels the same push.

items.p: How far down something is below the top of the water is called its ____.
items.why: Depth is the distance below the surface. The push of water grows with it.

items.p: Water that is free to flow in joined containers settles at the same ____ in all of them.
items.why: The level is the height of the water's surface. In joined containers, the water settles to the same level.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the push on each small part of a surface
how far down something is below the top of the water
a plunger that fits tightly in a tube
a wall across a river to hold water back
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Is the push of water bigger or smaller at each place, compared with a place 1 metre deep in a pond?
items: the bottom of a deep well
a fish just under the surface
a diver 20 metres down in the sea
the bottom of a tall water tank
a splash in a toddler's bath
items.a: see items
items.why: The push grows with depth. Places deeper than 1 metre have a bigger push, and shallower places have a smaller push.

items.p: A bottle has three holes at 4, 10 and 16 centimetres above its base. Put the jets in order from the weakest to the strongest.
items.why: The hole nearest the top has the least water above it, so it has the weakest jet. The lowest hole has the most water above it, so it has the strongest.

items.p: A friend says water only pushes downwards. Describe one way to show her that water pushes sideways too.
items.a: Make holes in the side of a bottle and fill it with water. The water shoots out sideways, so the water pushes on the side wall.
items.why: A strong answer names a test, such as holes in the side of a bottle, and says what it shows.

items.p: A roof tank is nearly empty, and the tap just below it runs slowly. Explain why in your own words.
items.a: The push at the tap comes from the depth of the water above it. When the tank is nearly empty, there is little depth of water above the tap, so the push is small and the water runs slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says the push depends on the depth of the water above the tap, and that the tank is shallow when nearly empty.

items.p: Draw a tall tank of water, seen from the side. Draw arrows to show the push on the side wall at three depths.
items.a: A tank with three arrows pointing outwards at the wall. The arrow near the top is short and the arrow near the bottom is the longest.
items.why: A strong drawing has longer arrows at the greater depths, because the push grows with depth.
items.art: A tall empty rectangle, like the side view of a tank.

items.p: In a bottle with holes at different heights, the lowest hole gives the strongest jet because there is more water above it.
items.why: True. The push grows with depth, and the lowest hole has the most water above it.

items.p: A tank and a thin tube are both filled with water to a depth of 3 metres. Which has the bigger push on each bit of its bottom?
items.why: The push depends only on the depth. The tank pushes on a bigger area, so its total force is bigger, but each bit feels the same push.

items.p: A bottle with three holes stands on the floor, and the lowest jet lands very short. Why?
opts: It has little height to fall, so it has little time in the air
items.why: The lowest jet leaves fast, but it starts close to the floor, so it lands soon. On a stool, it has time to travel farther.

items.p: 20 centimetres of coconut oil pushes less on the bottom of a jar than 20 centimetres of water, though coconut oil is thicker. Why?
opts: Coconut oil is lighter for its size
items.why: The push comes from the weight of the liquid above. Oil is lighter than water for the same amount. How thick or runny a liquid is does not change the pressure.

items.p: A small piston of 2 square centimetres is pushed with a force of 10 newtons. It is joined by oil to a big piston of 20 square centimetres. What force does the big piston give?
items.why: The pressure is the same everywhere. A piston with 10 times the area gets 10 times the force, so 10 times 10 is 100 newtons.

items.p: A car's brake pedal feels soft and spongy. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Air is squashed, so some of the push goes into squeezing the air and less reaches the brakes. Mechanics get rid of the air by bleeding the brakes.

items.p: A fountain is fed by a tank on a hill. What is true about the water jet?
opts: It cannot rise above the level of the water in the tank
It can rise twice as high as the tank
It rises higher if the tank is wider
items.why: All the push comes from the depth of water in the tank. The jet cannot rise above the level of the water that feeds it.

items.p: If you make a tank twice as wide, with the same depth of water, the pressure at its bottom doubles.
items.why: False. The pressure depends on the depth, not the width. The total force on the bottom doubles, because the area is twice as big, but each bit feels the same push.

items.p: At 10 metres under water, the total push is about double the push at the surface.
items.why: True. The air adds about one unit of push, and every 10 metres of water adds about one more.

items.p: A machine that uses a liquid in a closed pipe to pass on a push is called a ____ machine.
items.why: Hydraulic machines include car brakes, jacks and excavator arms.

items.p: Is each of these because the push of water grows with depth, or not?
items: Ears hurt in the deep end of a pool
A dam is thicker at the bottom
A top-floor tap is weak when the tank is low
A submarine for the deep sea has thick walls
items.a: see items
items.why: The push grows with depth, and that explains ears, dams, taps and submarines. Ice floating is about density, and honey is about thickness.

items.p: Match each machine to how it uses a liquid.
pairs: A foot pushes fluid, which pushes the pads on the wheel
A pump pushes fluid along tubes to move a piston
Pumping a handle pushes fluid under the seat to raise it
A thumb pushes the plunger, which pushes the liquid out of the tip
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: All four pass a push through a liquid, but the first three are hydraulic machines.

items.p: Put the steps of marking a level line with a hose in order.
items: Wait until the water stops moving
Hold the two ends against the wall
Fill the hose with water, with no bubbles
Mark the water level at each end
a: Fill the hose with water, with no bubbles
Hold the two ends against the wall
Wait until the water stops moving
Mark the water level at each end
items.why: First the hose must be full, then held in place, then left to settle, and only then marked.

items.p: A tall thin tube of water, filled to the top, can burst a strong barrel at its base. Explain how.
items.a: The push at the base depends on the depth of the water, and a tall tube is very deep. The barrel has a big area, so the push on all of it adds up to a big force that can burst it.
items.why: A strong answer says the pressure depends on the depth, and the push on the whole of a big area gives a big force.

items.p: A friend says a bigger water tank always gives a stronger tap. Give a reason why she may be wrong.
items.a: A tank that is wide but shallow has little depth of water above the tap. The push depends on the depth, not on the size of the tank.
items.why: A strong answer says the push depends on the depth of water above the tap.

items.p: Explain what 'water finds its own level' means, and give one example from home.
items.a: It means that water in joined containers settles at the same height. For example, the water in a kettle's spout stands as high as the water in its body.
items.why: A strong answer gives a correct example, such as a kettle, a hose or a pipe joining tanks.

items.p: Draw a kettle with water in it. Show the water level in the body and in the spout.
items.a: A kettle with the water at the same height in the spout and in the body, shown by a line across both.
items.why: A strong drawing has the water at the same height in the spout and the body.
items.art: An empty kettle outline with a body and a spout.

items.p: Rani and Imran are talking about a wide lake and a narrow tube of water that are both 5 metres deep.

views.says: The lake has far more water, so it must push harder on its bottom.
Only the depth counts, so each bit of the bottom feels the same push in the lake and in the tube.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing that the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Imran, because pressure depends only on depth, and both are 5 metres deep. It also says Rani is right that the lake has a much bigger total force, because it pushes on a much bigger area.
items.why: Both have a point. The push on each bit is the same, as Imran says. But the whole lake bed is far bigger, so the total force is bigger, as Rani feels.

items.p: A dam holds back water 30 metres deep. Not counting the air, about how many times the push of the air is the push of the water at the bottom?
items.why: Every 10 metres of water adds about the push of the air. 30 divided by 10 is 3, so the water at the bottom pushes about 3 times as hard as the air does.

items.p: A diver is 20 metres down in the sea. Counting the air above, about how many times the surface push does the diver feel?
items.why: The air adds 1 unit. Each 10 metres of water adds about 1 more, so 20 metres adds 2. The total is 3 times.

items.p: A tank of water on a hill feeds a fountain nozzle 5 metres below the water level. At most, about how high above the nozzle can the jet go?
items.why: A jet can rise at most to the level of the water that feeds it, apart from small splashes. That is 5 metres above the nozzle.

items.p: A bucket has one hole 8 centimetres below the water surface and another 2 centimetres below. How do the speeds of the two jets compare?
items.why: The push is bigger at the deeper hole, so the water leaves it faster.

items.p: A giraffe has a very high blood pressure. What is the best reason?
opts: Her heart has to push blood up her long neck to her head
items.why: Blood is a liquid, and the push needed to lift it grows with the height. A long neck needs a high pressure from the heart.

items.p: A hydraulic machine can lift a heavy load with a small push and also with a small movement.
items.why: False. A small push on a small piston gives a big force on a big piston, but the big piston moves much less. You trade distance for force.

items.p: In a hydraulic machine, a piston with 100 times the area gets ____ times the force.
items.why: The same pressure on 100 times the area gives 100 times the force.

items.p: In the three jets test, which things should be kept the same and which should change?
items.a: see items
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes, here the height of the hole. All the rest is kept the same.

items.p: Put these places in order from the smallest total push to the biggest total push.
items: The top of a high mountain
a: The top of a high mountain
items.why: On a mountain there is less air above, so the push is smaller. At sea level the air pushes about 1 unit. Under 10 metres of water the total is about 2 units.

items.p: A top-floor tap runs well when the roof tank is full and weakly when it is nearly empty. A ground-floor tap is strong either way. Explain both.
items.a: The top-floor tap is only a little below the tank, so the depth of water above it changes a lot when the tank empties. The ground-floor tap is far below the tank, so even a nearly empty tank adds little change to the depth above it.
items.why: A strong answer compares the depth above each tap and says why the change matters more near the top.

items.p: A small push on a small piston can lift a car when joined to a big piston. Explain how it works and what you give up.
items.a: The same pressure goes everywhere in the liquid, so a big piston gets a big force. But the big piston moves much less than the small one, so you give up distance.
items.why: A strong answer says the pressure is the same, the force grows with the area, and the distance moved shrinks.

items.p: Why must a submarine that dives very deep have very thick walls?
items.a: The push of the water grows with depth, and at great depths it is huge. The walls must be strong enough not to be crushed.
items.why: A strong answer links depth to a bigger push, and says the hull must be strong.

items.p: A friend says a siphon works because the air 'sucks' the water along. What would you tell her, and what do scientists still argue about?
items.a: The water is pushed by the air outside and pulled by gravity on the longer side. Scientists still argue about how much comes from the air pressure, and how much from the water pulling itself along.
items.why: A strong answer says sucking is not a push, and mentions the argument between the air-pressure view and the chain view.

items.p: Draw a bottle with three jets from three holes. Show which jet is longest, and label which hole has the deepest water above it.
items.a: A bottle with three arcs. The jet from the lowest hole is longest. The lowest hole is labelled as having the deepest water above it.
items.why: A strong drawing has the lowest hole giving the longest jet, and labels it as having the deepest water.
items.art: A tall empty bottle outline with three small circles for holes.

items.p: Draw two joined syringes with a small piston and a big piston. Show the push on each with arrows.
items.a: A small syringe and a big syringe joined by a tube. A short arrow on the small piston and a long arrow on the big piston.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a longer arrow on the big piston, because it gets a bigger force.
items.art: Two empty syringe outlines of different widths joined by a line.

items.p: Meena and Joseph disagree about a tall flat building where the top-floor tap is weak.

views.says: Put the water tank on a higher stand, so the water is deeper above the top taps.
Put a pump on the pipe, so the water is pushed even when the tank is low.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing that the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason about pressure. For Meena, the push comes from the depth above the tap. For Joseph, a pump adds a push that does not depend on the tank. It also says that the other idea would work too.
items.why: Both work, because both raise the push at the tap. A higher tank uses depth of water, and a pump adds its own push. Which is better depends on cost, space and electricity.

applications: Overhead tanks on roofs send water down to taps by the push of their own water, and the higher the tank, the stronger the push.
Hydraulic brakes in cars, autos and lorries pass a foot's push through a liquid to the wheels.
Excavators such as JCBs lift tonnes of soil with liquid pushed along tubes to pistons.
A barber's chair, a car jack and a garage lift all use a hydraulic piston to lift a load with a small push.
Dams are built thickest at the bottom, where the push of the water is the biggest.
Masons use a clear hose of water to mark a level line on a long wall.
Water towers in towns are built high, so that taps far away still get a good push of water.
Submarines and deep-sea research vehicles have thick, strong hulls to survive the huge push of the sea at depth.
Blood pressure cuffs measure the push of blood in the arteries, which doctors use to check on health.
Diving tables tell divers how long they can stay at each depth, because the push of the water changes the gases in their blood.
Hydroelectric power stations use the push of deep water behind a dam to spin turbines.
Drip irrigation tanks raised on a stand give a steady push to water in tubes across a field.

open_questions.q: How does a siphon work: by air pressure, or by the water pulling itself along?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments in recent years have reported siphons running in a vacuum. Scientists still argue about how much comes from each cause.

open_questions.q: Why does water flow smoothly in some places and become a swirling, chaotic mess in others?
open_questions.why_open: The way a fluid turns from smooth to turbulent is still not fully explained, and it is one of the big unsolved problems in physics.

open_questions.q: How do deep-sea animals keep their bodies working under a push more than a thousand times that of the air?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that some deep-sea fish use special chemicals in their cells, but there is a lot more to learn about how they cope.

open_questions.q: Is there liquid water in oceans under the ice of other worlds, and what is the pressure like there?
open_questions.why_open: Some moons of Jupiter and Saturn seem to have oceans under their ice. Space missions are being planned to find out more.

open_questions.q: Is the pressure at the very centre of the Earth really millions of times the surface air pressure?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists work out the pressure from the weight of the rock above and from how earthquake waves travel. They have no way to measure it directly.

open_questions.q: How did people thousands of years ago know how to build dams and step wells without knowing the rule of pressure?
open_questions.why_open: Few written records tell us how the builders learned. Historians think they learned from many trials and failures.

maths.context: This is about the three jets test, with made-up results.
maths.problem: The top jet landed 37 centimetres away, the middle jet 46 centimetres and the bottom jet 52 centimetres. How much farther did the bottom jet go than the top jet? How much farther than the middle jet?
maths.answer: 15 centimetres farther than the top jet, and 6 centimetres farther than the middle jet.
maths.explain: 52 take away 37 is 15. 52 take away 46 is 6. The bottom jet beat the top jet by 15 centimetres, and the middle jet by 6 centimetres.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the distances shows how much each hole's jet beat the others, in a way you can compare.

maths.context: This is about the three jets test again, with the same made-up results.
maths.problem: The bottom hole was 18 centimetres below the water line and the top hole was 6 centimetres below. How many times as deep is the bottom hole? The bottom jet landed 52 centimetres away and the top jet 37 centimetres away. Is the bottom jet 3 times as far? Why might that be?
maths.answer: 3 times as deep. The bottom jet is only about 1.4 times as far.
maths.explain: 18 divided by 6 is 3, so the bottom hole is 3 times as deep. 52 divided by 37 is about 1.4. The jet does not go 3 times as far. Three times the depth gives a faster jet, but the speed grows more slowly than the depth, and the jet also has to fall to the floor.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two ratios shows that a result can grow more slowly than the thing that causes it.

maths.context: This is about the three tries in the jets test.
maths.problem: Three tries for the bottom hole landed at 50, 54 and 52 centimetres. What is the middle number? Why use the middle number and not the biggest?
maths.answer: 52 centimetres. The biggest might be a fluke.
maths.explain: Put the numbers in order: 50, 52, 54. The middle one is 52. One try can be a fluke, so the middle number is fairer than the biggest or smallest.
maths.why_maths: Using the middle number makes a result more trustworthy when each try is a little different.

maths.context: This is about the level line test with a hose.
maths.problem: The first mark was 101.2 centimetres above the floor and the second mark was 101.5 centimetres above the floor, 3 metres away. What is the difference in centimetres and in millimetres? How many millimetres is that for each metre of the wall?
maths.answer: 0.3 centimetres, which is 3 millimetres. That is 1 millimetre for each metre.
maths.explain: 101.5 take away 101.2 is 0.3 centimetres. There are 10 millimetres in a centimetre, so 0.3 centimetres is 3 millimetres. The wall is 3 metres long, and 3 divided by 3 is 1 millimetre in each metre.
maths.why_maths: Changing to millimetres and sharing along the wall shows how small the error is.

maths.context: This is about the tap survey.
maths.problem: The kitchen tap filled a 1 litre bottle in 12 seconds, and the shower filled it in 48 seconds. How many times as fast is the kitchen tap? How many litres in a minute does each give?
maths.answer: 4 times as fast. The kitchen tap gives 5 litres a minute and the shower 1.25 litres a minute.
maths.explain: 48 divided by 12 is 4. A minute has 60 seconds. 60 divided by 12 is 5 litres a minute. 60 divided by 48 is 1.25 litres a minute.
maths.why_maths: Turning seconds for one litre into litres a minute lets you compare taps fairly.

maths.context: This is about the syringe arm project.
maths.problem: A small syringe has a piston with an area of 1 square centimetre. A bigger one has an area of 4 square centimetres. They are joined by water. You push the small piston with a force of 3 newtons. What force does the big piston get? If the small piston moves 8 centimetres, how far does the big one move?
maths.answer: 12 newtons. The big piston moves 2 centimetres.
maths.explain: The pressure is the same in both. Four times the area gives four times the force, so 3 times 4 is 12 newtons. The same amount of water moves a piston with four times the area one quarter as far, so 8 divided by 4 is 2 centimetres.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the force and dividing the distance by the same number shows the trade you make with a hydraulic machine.

maths.context: This is about a roof tank like the ones in the unit.
maths.problem: A roof tank is 2 metres long, 1.5 metres wide and 1 metre deep. How many cubic metres does it hold? One cubic metre holds 1,000 litres. How many litres is that? By 7 in the morning, three quarters of the water has been used. How many litres are left?
maths.answer: 3 cubic metres, which is 3,000 litres. 750 litres are left.
maths.explain: 2 times 1.5 is 3, and 3 times 1 is 3 cubic metres. 3 times 1,000 is 3,000 litres. Three quarters of 3,000 is 2,250, so 3,000 take away 2,250 leaves 750 litres. Only a quarter is left, so the water is shallow.
maths.why_maths: Fractions of a tank show how little depth is left when most of the water has been used.

maths.context: This is about the push of the sea at depth.
maths.problem: Every 10 metres of water adds about one unit of push, and the air adds one unit. At 10 metres, the total push is 2 units. What is the total at 30 metres? How many times as deep is 30 metres as 10 metres? How many times as big is the total push?
maths.answer: 4 units at 30 metres. 3 times as deep, but only 2 times the total push.
maths.explain: At 30 metres the water adds 3 units, and the air adds 1, so the total is 4. 30 divided by 10 is 3 times as deep. 4 divided by 2 is 2 times the total. The air always adds one unit, so the total does not grow as fast as the depth.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the depth with the total push shows why you must count the air as well as the water.

maths.context: This is about the dam drawing.
maths.problem: You draw a dam 30 metres tall, with 1 centimetre of drawing for every 5 metres. How tall is the drawing of the dam? The dam is 20 metres thick at its base. How thick is the base in the drawing?
maths.answer: 6 centimetres tall. 4 centimetres thick at the base.
maths.explain: 30 divided by 5 is 6 centimetres. 20 divided by 5 is 4 centimetres. Each centimetre in the drawing stands for 5 metres in the real dam.
maths.why_maths: A scale drawing lets you fit a huge dam on a page and keep its shape.

roots.context: We have measured the push of water at different depths and watched water find its level in a hose. Now we ask what it means that a place in water is held only by the water above it, and what that says about us.

deep_truth.truth: In the bottle test, the lowest hole squirted farthest, though all three holes met the same water. In the hose test, a thin tube and a wide bucket stood at the same height. A place in water is pushed only by the water above it. How much water lies around it makes no difference.
deep_truth.habit: We think more water means more push, so that a big tank beats a small one and a wide lake beats a thin tube. The tests show that depth matters, and the amount does not.
deep_truth.evidence: In the bottle test, the jets from the deeper holes landed farther. In the hose test, the water in the wide funnel and the thin tube stood at the same height. If your results differ, write them down as they are.

three.who_am_i: Your blood is a liquid too. When you stand, the push in your feet is bigger than in your head, just as a lower hole in the bottle pushes harder than a higher one.
three.what_is_life: A fish feels the push of the water all over her body, and it grows as she swims deeper. Scientists think deep-diving whales let their lungs fold flat as they go down.
three.what_is_this_world: The sea, the rain in the clouds and the water in a tank all follow the same rule. The deeper you go, the more water lies above you, and the more it pushes.

roots.thread: Gravity pulls on every bit of water, and the water below must hold up the water above. So the push grows with depth, and it is the same in every direction at one depth. A bottle, a dam and a hose all follow this one rule. Water settles to one level whenever it can flow freely, because only then is the push equal at equal depths.

teachings.teaching: The deeper you dig in sandy ground, the more water springs up. In the same way, the more you learn, the more knowledge springs up in you. Scholars do not agree on the date of the Kural, and some place it about two thousand years ago.
teachings.link: The deeper the well, the stronger the push of the water at the bottom. Deeper means more push, which is the same rule you saw in the bottle test.

teachings.teaching: The rivers and the seas are lords of the valley streams because they are good at staying below them. So the streams flow to them.
teachings.link: Water always runs down to the lowest place, and the deepest water there pushes hardest. The sea is the lowest place, and all rivers find their way to it.

science.text: The pressure in a liquid grows with depth, and at one depth it is the same in every direction.
A change of pressure at one place in a closed liquid is passed on equally to every other place.
How a siphon works is still argued, between the push of the air and the pull of water on itself.

other_view.view: Pressure is a number that you work out from the depth and the weight of the liquid. To say that a place in the water is held up by the water above it is a helpful picture, but it adds nothing to the maths, and it should not be read as a lesson about anything else.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells how people found out that the push of water depends on depth, and not on how much water there is.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought that more water must push harder at the bottom. A wide lake, they said, must press on its bed far harder than a bucket does. In 1586, a Flemish engineer named Simon Stevin reasoned and showed that this is not so. The push on the bottom depends on how deep the water is, and not on how much water there is or on the shape of the vessel. About sixty years later, the French thinker Blaise Pascal went further. He showed that a push on a liquid in a closed container goes out equally in every direction. A famous story says that Pascal fixed a long thin tube to a sealed barrel of water and poured a few cups of water into the tube. The barrel is said to have burst. The story may be a legend, but the physics is right: a tall thin tube of water pushes on its bottom as much as a tall wide tank does.
how_we_found_out.who: Simon Stevin, a Flemish engineer, and Blaise Pascal, a French thinker
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought that a bigger amount of water, or a wider container, must push harder at the bottom. Stevin and Pascal showed that only the depth matters, and that a push on a closed liquid goes everywhere equally.
